title: Pro Football Hall of Fame Game 2026 watch guide: What to know about Panthers vs. Cardinals Larry Fitzgerald, Luke Kuechly and the rest of the 2026 Hall of Fame class will be honored before kickoff. Here's how to tune in. Steven Louis Goldstein 6
summary:
Backup Kenny Pickett is slated as Carolina's starting quarterback for Thursday. Matt Kelley / Getty Images
For the first time since February’s Super Bowl, two NFL teams are lining up for all to see. Huzzahs are in order.
The NFL inches closer to its regular season with the annual Hall of Fame Game. Thursday’s preseason opener pairs the Arizona Cardinals and Carolina Panthers, as new gold-jacketers Larry Fitzgerald and Luke Kuechly look on before their Pro Football Hall of Fame induction on Satur
full_text:
Backup Kenny Pickett is slated as Carolina's starting quarterback for Thursday. Matt Kelley / Getty Images
For the first time since February’s Super Bowl, two NFL teams are lining up for all to see. Huzzahs are in order.
The NFL inches closer to its regular season with the annual Hall of Fame Game. Thursday’s preseason opener pairs the Arizona Cardinals and Carolina Panthers, as new gold-jacketers Larry Fitzgerald and Luke Kuechly look on before their Pro Football Hall of Fame induction on Saturday. Here’s what to know and where to tune in.
* depending on local market
NBC is free over the air and streams with a Peacock subscription. This game is also available on mobile through NFL+.
Fitzgerald and Kuechly are going to be honored before kickoff, along with the other members of the 2026 Hall of Fame class. Quarterback Drew Brees, running back Roger Craig and kicker Adam Vinatieri round out this year’s inductees. Some of them will be interviewed during the pregame show or the game itself.
The Hall of Fame Game gets the NBC “Sunday Night Football” broadcast crew. Mike Tirico calls play-by-play, Cris Collinsworth is on analysis and Melissa Stark handles sideline updates and interviews.
The on-site “Football Night in America” pregame starts at 7 p.m. ET. It marks the studio introduction for longtime Pittsburgh Steelers coach Mike Tomlin. He joins Mike Florio, Jason Garrett, Devin McCourty and host Maria Taylor.
Few (if any) starters are suiting up Thursday night, but it’s still a meaningful look for players in pursuit of roster spots.
Arizona is the nominal home team in Canton. It’s the unofficial debut for first-year head coach Mike LaFleur, who leads the Cardinals after three seasons as offensive coordinator of the Los Angeles Rams. LaFleur’s offense ranked No. 1 in both points and yards last year. He inherits a team in transition — former franchise quarterback Kyler Murray is now with the Minnesota Vikings, while rookie running back Jeremiyah Love arrives as the No. 3 pick in April’s draft.
Fellow rookie Carson Beck will start under center. A third-round draft pick, Beck joins Arizona following a run to the College Football Playoff title game with Miami. He is third on the Cardinals’ preseason depth chart behind Jacoby Brissett and Gardner Minshew II.
Carolina counters with backup Kenny Pickett at QB in place of usual starter Bryce Young. Pickett went 20th overall in the 2022 draft and compiled a 14-10 record with the Steelers. He’s been a traveling backup for the past two seasons, spending 2024 with the Philadelphia Eagles and 2025 with the Las Vegas Raiders.
Dave Canales begins his third campaign as head coach of the Panthers. His team improved from 5-12 in 2024 to 8-9 and a division title last year. The Panthers hosted the Rams for a wild-card playoff thriller , which they lost 34-31 despite heroic efforts from Young and receiver Jalen Coker.
Arizona is 1-3-1 in five previous Canton contests. It was a part of the inaugural Hall of Fame Game back in 1962, when the franchise was still based in St. Louis. That game ended as a 21-21 tie with the New York Giants.
The Cardinals were last here for the 2017 game. That year’s Hall of Fame class included Kurt Warner, who led Arizona to its lone Super Bowl appearance in the 2008 season.
Carolina is 1-0 in the Hall of Fame Game. The Panthers and Jacksonville Jaguars played in the 1995 exhibition as brand-new franchises. Carolina won 20-14 thanks to an inspired goal-line stand in the final minutes. Future two-time Super Bowl champion Tyrone Poole also took an interception 85 yards to the house, which galvanized the sold-out crowd.
These are the honorees who have contributed to each franchise — as players, coaches, team owners or executives. Names are sorted alphabetically.
Courtesy of The Athletic ‘s Katie Richcreek , deputing managing editor of sports betting:
These odds are within the range of what we would expect to see for the Hall of Fame Game.
The Cardinals and Panthers are only two weeks into training camp, and as is the case for the rest of the NFL preseason, starters will see limited playing time. That’s why Carolina is a modest moneyline favorite with around a 55 percent implied probability to win, and has only a 1.5-point edge on the spread. There hasn’t been a spread bigger than a field goal since 2015.
The over/under is higher than recent history; a Hall of Fame Game total hasn’t opened or closed above 35 points since 2019. Half of the last 10 Hall of Fame Game matchups went over.
The coin-flip nature of these odds reflect the coin-flop nature of this game — and why we’ll be staying away from betting it.

full_text:
Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen has to sort out the secondary with safety Coby Bryant and nickelback Kyler Gordon sidelined. Kamil Krzaczynski / Imagn Images
Dennis Allen knew the barrage was coming, a flurry of “What now?” questions awaiting as he began his first full day of troubleshooting after the Chicago Bears lost safety Coby Bryant to a significant knee injury this week. Allen knew it would be months before he’d again have Bryant available on his chessboard and that his homework had just intensified.
Thus, when he entered the Halas Hall media room 45 minutes ahead of Tuesday morning’s practice, he flashed a knowing grin and threw both hands onto the lectern.
“Go ahead, guys,” Allen said, bypassing any opening statement and diving right into the Bryant problem.
For the next five minutes, the queries came rapid fire.
What was Allen’s emotional reaction after Bryant suffered a knee hyperextension and bone bruise during Monday’s padded practice, injuries likely to sideline him well into October?
Who’s the next man up in the Bears’ secondary?
What does this mean for rookie safety Dillon Thieneman?
And how might the ripple effect of Bryant’s absence also impact fourth-round pick Malik Muhammad?
“Nothing ever goes exactly how you planned, right?” Allen said. “You have to be able to adjust. You have to be able to change course when needed. It’s just part of what we do.”
So Allen vowed to lean into his problem-solving experience to steer the Bears through these choppy waters. And most importantly, as he had already done with the entire defensive unit, he delivered a tone-setting message.
“Everybody asks, ‘What do you want to see out of this guy? What do you want to see out of that guy? What do you want to see out of this guy?’” Allen said. “You know what I want to see? I want to see 11 frickin’ dudes on the field competing their asses off. If we all do that, I feel pretty confident we’ll get them to the right spot.”
Just like that, purpose had been re-established for the defense even with acknowledgment that Bryant’s exit for the foreseeable future will be a significant blow.
Bryant, after all, had quickly established himself at Halas Hall as a dynamic playmaker and leader, a Super Bowl champion with the Seahawks who had drawn praise throughout the spring and into the early days of training camp for his aggressive playing style.
“Obviously it sucks to lose a guy like that for any particular time,” Allen said. “He’s a big part of what we have planned to do.”
Added linebacker Devin Bush: “In this life of football, you never know what happens. Obviously, whoever’s backing him up has to step up now.”
Enter Cam Lewis, himself a newcomer after joining the Bears in free agency in March following seven seasons in Buffalo. Lewis’ scouting report is solid but not spectacular. Smart. Instinctive. Versatile. He’s been a special teams standout and a spot starter. But he’s the kind of selfless, multi-dimensional player teams love to keep around in case of an emergency.
The problem is, ahead of even the first preseason game, the Bears have needed to lean on Lewis for two emergencies. First, he had been called upon to fill in at nickel corner, plugging a hole there as Kyler Gordon’s indefinite stint on the physically unable to perform (PUP) list with a calf injury drags on.
Now, Lewis is needed even more at safety, with Thieneman leaning into his new partner’s experience.
“He definitely knows how to play in the back end, knows different tendencies, knows how to work well with other guys,” Thieneman said. “He’s another guy I’ve been asking questions, just to get his viewpoint on the game.”
Bryant’s injury leaves the Bears even thinner at safety with Elijah Hicks (shin) also carrying a PUP designation through the early stages of camp. The depth pieces at that position aren’t exactly household names.
• Anthony Johnson Jr. — fourth-year vet, four career starts, on his third team.
• Skyler Thomas — undrafted rookie from Oregon State.
• Gervarrius Owens — fourth-year vet, fourth team, has been mostly a practice-squad guy.
Thieneman, meanwhile, has worked into the spotlight, flashing the play speed and feel for the game the Bears fell in love with during the pre-draft process. But he also has participated in all of two NFL padded practices to this point with a flood of information still coming at him.
“There’s a lot to learn in the National Football League,” Allen said. “There is a lot going on. The volume of what we do is more than what most rookies have ever done before. The volume of what they’re seeing from our offense is (also) going to be more than what they’re used to seeing.”
In other words, the Bears are taking a patient approach and keeping early expectations with Thieneman measured.
“Everything’s starting to slow down,” Thieneman said. “I’m starting to pick up things, (understand) tendencies from the offense and just building more connection with the guys on defense.”
And Muhammad? Well, he’s again receiving trial reps at slot cornerback, pushed to heighten the competition there, which also includes Jaylon Jones and Josh Blackwell.
As he cross-trains inside, Muhammad will need to show sharpened anticipation, fast reaction time and good vision. Growing pains are expected.
“I want to see him go out and perform,” Allen said. “I want to see him go out and compete. I want to see him play physical in the run game. I want to see him be sticky in coverage.”
The arrival of Week 1 is now barely four weeks away. The clock is ticking for the defense to find answers.
Still, most of August is left for the Bears to attack their to-do lists, to continue navigating around obstacles both big and small and to learn who they want to be.
Allen will wish for the quickest possible return for Bryant. At the same time, he remains on a mission to get 11 frickin’ dudes competing their asses off.
“That’s what this time of year is all about,” Allen said. “This is about developing the culture and the way you’re going to play.”
Even if that task became significantly more difficult this week.

full_text:
Colts RB Jonathan Taylor led the league in touchdowns last season with 20. Mike Carlson / Getty Images
The Athletic has live coverage of NFL training camp .
Jonathan Taylor said he wanted to be an Indianapolis “Colt for life.” Now the star running back is one step closer to turning that dream into reality. Taylor agreed to a two-year, $44 million contract extension Thursday with the Colts, according to league sources who spoke anonymously because they were not authorized to speak publicly. The deal is worth up to $47 million and includes $39 million guaranteed. Taylor will now be under contract through the 2028 season.
Taylor was entering the final year of a three-year, $42 million contract extension he inked in October 2023. That lucrative deal came after a public and sometimes bitter back-and-forth between Taylor and his agent, Malki Kawa, and late Colts owner Jim Irsay. Taylor and Irsay even exchanged verbal jabs via social media before Taylor landed a new deal. This time around, the negotiations went a lot smoother, as the 2020 second-round pick participated in training camp and was rewarded with a third contract from the team that drafted him, which is an increasing rarity for running backs.
The new deal puts Taylor at $22 million in terms of average annual salary, second among running backs. He trails only the Atlanta Falcons’ Bijan Robinson ($22.25 million).
Robinson agreed to a three-year , $66.8 million deal Tuesday. Taylor was notified of Robinson’s contract after practice, and while he said he was thrilled for another running back to get paid, he also acknowledged his own negotiations.
“I gotta go talk to my agent, too,” Taylor said Tuesday. “… I have faith, so I’m gonna tap in and check in with him, now that you guys broke the news to me.”
Two days later, Taylor was rewarded with a new contract. The agreement is not a surprise since Colts principal owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon and GM Chris Ballard have praised Taylor this offseason. Both referred to him as a franchise pillar.
“I’d definitely love to be a Colt for life. I think I’ve already expressed that to them throughout the years,” Taylor said during minicamp in June. “… Hopefully they feel the same (way) because this is a special place. Not every building is like this, and I’ve heard some stories now, especially from guys coming from other places, and it’s not like this elsewhere.”
Taylor, 27, is coming off an impressive 2025 campaign that at one point had him in the league MVP conversation. He appeared in every game and registered 1,585 rushing yards, his most in a season since earning a first-team All-Pro nod in 2021. Additionally, Taylor’s league-leading 20 total touchdowns (18 rushing and two receiving) last year are tied with Hall of Famer Lenny Moore for the most in a single season in Colts history. Taylor is the only Colts player to reach that threshold twice (2021 and 2025).
Taylor’s new deal confirms that the Colts view him as a part of their long-term future, even if the man who brought him to Indianapolis may not be around. Ballard is entering the final year of his contract, and it’s fair to consider that if Indianapolis misses the playoffs for a sixth straight season, Ballard could be relieved of his duties.
Ballard traded up three spots to select Taylor with the No. 41 pick in the second round of the 2020 NFL Draft. The former Wisconsin standout has had some durability issues throughout his pro career, missing at least three games in each of the 2022, 2023 and 2024 seasons. Despite those absences, Taylor has still emerged as one of the league’s premier running backs.
Taylor’s career average of 90.5 rushing yards per game is the most among active players and ranks fifth all-time behind Hall of Famers Jim Brown, Barry Sanders, Terrell Davis and Eric Dickerson, respectively. Taylor, a three-time Pro Bowler, ranks first in Colts history with 69 rushing TDs. His 7,598 rushing yards are second in franchise history only to Hall of Famer Edgerrin James (9,226).

WESTFIELD, Ind. — Even Rick Venturi knows he’s telling a lie, albeit a benign one. The former Indianapolis Colts coach and current radio analyst always says he’ll be a “little” early for the start of training camp practice. But Tuesday, he arrives at 9:16 a.m., a full 44 minutes before the action gets underway. Typical.
As Venturi sits down in a chair facing the Colts’ two practice fields at Grand Park, the grass is still relatively empty, with only a few coaches and players beating him there. But from Venturi’s perspective, there’s no use in waiting any longer. The 80-year-old football lifer, whom The Athletic shadowed for Tuesday’s practice, has already been up since 4:30 a.m., fueled by his unwavering love for the game.
“I’ve always been an early riser. I keep the hours of a farmer to tell you the truth,” Venturi says, laughing. “And the reason for that is, after I get some coffee in me, that’s when I think the clearest. There are no distractions, no phone. I’m just unimpeded in my man cave, watching tape, writing reports, getting my podcast ready or getting ready for the game.”
The only thing that interferes with Venturi’s all-football mornings is when he has to make coffee for his wife, Cheri, whom he affectionately calls “Mrs. Cheri.” She wakes up at about 9 a.m., he says, and that’s typically when he re-emerges from his basement to get to brewing.
Otherwise, Venturi still treats every day as if he’s the one calling the plays on the field rather than analyzing them from the press box. Venturi, who jokes he’s “80 going on 40” after having both of his knees replaced earlier this year, knows his coaching days are long gone, but internally, he can never turn it off.
“I was raised on it. My dad, Joe, was a Hall of Fame high school coach (in Illinois),” says Venturi, who wears his late father’s Hall of Fame ring every day to honor him. “When I was like 7 years old, I went on most of the trips with him. I was on the bus. I was on the sidelines. And I don’t say this egotistically, but because of my background, I could explain the split-T to the quarterbacks when I was 7. My dad would have me do that.”
Venturi loves sharing these stories of yesteryear, but when practice finally begins at 10 a.m., his focus shifts to the present. Here’s what he had to say about the Colts and what could lie ahead in 2026.
10:08 a.m. — The Colts’ kicking competition resumes with Spencer Shrader getting a turn, one day after Blake Grupe drilled all six of his field goal attempts. Shrader fails to hold serve, missing from 45 and 57 yards. Venturi takes note, acknowledging that though Shrader is still working his way back from a season-ending knee injury he suffered last October, the 5-foot-7 Grupe is leaving little doubt about who should be the Colts’ starting kicker.
Throughout training camp so far, Grupe is a perfect 12-of-12 on field goal attempts, and Shrader has missed three of his 12 tries. Last year, Grupe, who was cut by the New Orleans Saints after missing eight kicks in 11 games, replaced Shrader and has been unflappable in Indy.
“Grupe’s just mind-boggling,” Venturi says. “He’s undefeated. He hasn’t missed a kick. But my question is: Who was that guy in New Orleans? I don’t question if he’s good enough. I question how the hell he missed so many kicks!”
10:15 a.m. — Venturi yells to Colts pass game coordinator and secondary coach Chris Hewitt during a special teams period. Hewitt recognizes the voice, turns around and jogs over to give Venturi a hug. Venturi coached Hewitt, a former safety, with the Saints in the late 1990s. Now, Hewitt is tasked with coaching what Venturi believes is one of the most talented secondaries in Colts history, headlined by its cornerbacks.
Indianapolis has two All-Pros flanking each other on the outside, Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward Sr. The duo appeared in only one full game together last year because of a calf injury to Gardner and repeated concussions for Ward. Venturi is confident they can be one of the top outside duos in the league — if they stay healthy. He’s also high on second-year slot cornerback Justin Walley, who missed his entire rookie season because of a torn ACL.
“For Lou (Anarumo) to be at his best as a defensive coordinator, he needs his horses, and he’s got three of them,” Venturi says, noting the Colts allowed the third-most passing yards per game (247.9) in the NFL in 2025. “He didn’t really have these guys last year, so they weren’t able to play as much man-to-man as he wanted. You can’t play pure zone in this league and consistently win. The quarterbacks are too good.”
10:23 a.m. — Seth McGowan darts by during a running back drill. The rookie seventh-round pick, who stands 6 feet and weighs 223 pounds, is noticeably bigger than the rest of the players at his position. Venturi thinks there’s a real chance McGowan can be the Colts’ backup running back, especially if he can hold up in pass protection. McGowan, whom Venturi calls “the steal of the draft,” is competing with 2025 fifth-round pick DJ Giddens for the top reserve role.
“Jonathan Taylor is one of my very favorite players of all time, and I’ve seen a lot of them,” Venturi says, laughing. “But he can’t do it by himself. With McGowan, and even Giddens, we have to be able to trust you in the passing game. Danny Jones needs to be able to trust you. But with McGowan, he was very good at Kentucky. He’s not a jitterbug. He’s a one-cut guy. He’s got good vision, and he’ll put that shoulder down when he needs to get through (the hole).”
10:31 a.m. — The Colts begin their first 11-on-11 period down near the goal line. Second-year tight end Tyler Warren lines up in the backfield with Taylor before Jones fakes a handoff to Warren and then slings a short touchdown pass to Josh Downs. Venturi points out Warren’s versatility and how his mere presence on the field can bend a defense. Last year, Warren totaled 76 catches for 817 yards and four touchdowns in what Venturi considers arguably the best rookie tight end showing in franchise history.
“Despite the receiver situation, when you have Warren, who’s just a terrific hybrid player, you can still do some fun things,” Venturi says. “He can play at the edge as an old-fashioned tight end. That time, he was at fullback. He can even be your third wide receiver if you have two tight ends in the game. So, if you’re a defensive coordinator and Mo Alie-Cox and Warren are in the game, do you go nickel (with five defensive backs)? Or do you go base (with four defensive backs)? That eases your game plan a bit and gives you a lot of options and answers on offense.”
10:42 a.m. — Venturi beelines from one field to the other as the offensive linemen and defensive linemen do their one-on-ones. He can’t hide his excitement, repeatedly stating this is “where games are really won.” Venturi tips his cap to 2024 first-round pick Laiatu Latu, who easily whipped around second-year right tackle Jalen Travis for a “sack” in one of their first reps. He expects Latu to build on the 8.5 sacks he had last year, but that might be possible only if another defensive end steps up.
“Jaylahn (Tuimoloau) is the guy that’s gotta come through for us, at least on first down,” Venturi says as the 2025 second-round pick gets the best of backup tackle Luke Tenuta with a swim move. “I think you’re hoping that you can use him and (Arden) Key in conjunction, with (Tuimoloau) being your first-down guy, and Key being your designated pass rusher on third down.”
Last year, Tuimoloau didn’t record a single start or sack, but Venturi isn’t deterred by Tuimoloau’s lack of rookie-year production, noting the Colts had a few veterans playing ahead of Tuimoloau. This year, those guys are gone, leaving Tuimoloau with a great opportunity to earn more snaps.

full_text:
Chiefs cornerback Mansoor Delane, the No. 6 pick in April's draft, is not a full-go for practices because of a lingering shoulder injury. Denny Medley / Imagn Images
ST. JOSEPH, Mo. — The Kansas City Chiefs are officially a week into full-squad training camp, which means it’s a good time to look at things from a big-picture view.
Who’s standing out? And who has slipped on the depth chart since practices began?
Here’s a look at the Chiefs’ early risers and fallers.
It would be difficult to overstate the kind of underdog story it’d be if undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson becomes the Chiefs’ 2026 starting right tackle.
He isn’t just an undrafted rookie out of Indiana; he ended up signing with the Chiefs after he stood out among more than 100 tryout players at rookie minicamp. The odds of a player like that just making the roster are usually minuscule.
And yet … Benson has been the primary starter at right tackle during training camp while competing with veteran Jaylon Moore.
Benson, at 6 feet 6 and 319 pounds, still has a lot to prove. And he’s had some rough practice moments recently while going against what is increasingly looking like an improved K.C. defensive line.
But it’s also late enough in practices now to know Benson’s placement on the depth chart is more than a ploy to motivate Moore. Benson is getting a real look to start in Week 1, which means any Chiefs risers list has to include him.
I want to be clear: This isn’t an indictment of rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane, the player. But the longer the No. 6 pick is not a full-go for practices because of a lingering shoulder injury, the more worried I am about him being ready — mentally and physically — to start Week 1.
The Chiefs are trying to thread quite a needle here. Delane, while still wearing a yellow, no-contact jersey, has been out on the field to get mental reps during 11-on-11 drills before retreating to the sideline for the actual play. The setup indicates he’s eager to keep learning — and the Chiefs want to involve him as much as they can — but it also shows the team isn’t getting him the full integration they would’ve hoped.
There’s a lot of pressure here for Delane to work out … and right away. The team lacks depth at cornerback after trading Trent McDuffie and losing Jaylen Watson in free agency, and the fact K.C. used excess draft resources to trade up for him only solidifies the reality that he needs to be an immediate contributor.
Delane will be playing catch-up over the next few weeks even if he heals quickly, and that’s not ideal for a team that needs him ready early.
We haven’t seen much from second-year tight end Jake Briningstool, who took the equivalent of a redshirt season in 2025 while battling a hamstring injury.
The 2025 undrafted free agent put two of his best practices together in a row this week, though, earning some first-string reps with quarterback Patrick Mahomes on Wednesday while also impressing Tuesday with a twisting catch over the middle.
. @Garrettnuss13 ➡️ @Jbriningstool pic.twitter.com/r8qhVxDJm8
— Kansas City Chiefs (@Chiefs) August 4, 2026
Reid complimented Briningstool Wednesday for his recent progress.
“It’s great that he’s back-to-back in some practices here, and then you get a chance to see what he’s all about,” Reid said. “He’s a good receiver, and you know what? He’s stuck his nose in there, and he’s blocking. My hat goes off to him. He’s just got to keep stacking. That’s his challenge right now.”
Much like my take on Delane, I want to be clear about what I’m saying here.
The Chiefs were thrilled to get Emmett Johnson in the fifth round of April’s draft, and I’d think his long-term prospects with the team remain unchanged. But as of now … he’s been a clear fourth in the running back pecking order in practices, behind both Brashard Smith and Emari Demercado.
That doesn’t mean it can’t change, or that the Chiefs don’t have plans for him. At minimum, they appear to have plenty of special teams work slated for Johnson as he integrates into the pros.
Reid mentioned Wednesday that one thing the team needed to see more from Johnson was keeping his pad level low while running.
“You go high at this level, and you’re going to get rearranged,” Reid said. “And you don’t want that to happen.”
What we can say as of now: The Chiefs feel more comfortable with other options as Johnson continues to grow.
First-round defensive tackle Peter Woods was the clear standout of the first padded practice this week and continues to flash in one-on-one drills.
Woods said two weeks ago he slimmed down to 308 pounds while hoping to become the type of quick-fire mismatch he was early in his Clemson career. It’s still early in training camp, but I’d say Woods’ start has been the most encouraging of any defensive player.
Like Johnson above, this is only a depth-chart observation and not a final verdict on what fourth-round cornerback Jadon Canady will eventually become.
For now, though, Canady is behind Chris Roland-Wallace and free-agent signing Kader Kohou at slot cornerback. Canady should be a Day 1 special teams contributor, but he might need some time to crack the team’s top cornerback rotation.
The Chiefs do not appear to have extensive depth at defensive end, so 2023 first-round pick Felix Anudike-Uzomah’s having his best camp has been a welcome storyline, especially with second-year player Ashton Gillotte missing recent practices with a hamstring injury.
Anudike-Uzomah, who missed last season with a hamstring injury, has held his own during first-team reps while impressing Reid with his explosiveness.
“Way different getting off the ball,” Reid said Wednesday of Anudike-Uzomah. “If there’s one thing that jumps out at you, it’s that.”
Though Anudike-Uzomah has had a disappointing Chiefs career, he’s still just 24 as he enters the final season of his rookie deal. While it’d be silly to predict a double-digit-sack season, it remains true that Anudike-Uzomah would exceed expectations if he simply brought some pass-rush juice while serving as a capable rotation player on the defensive line.
The way he’s played so far, he’s trending toward clearing that benchmark with ease.
• Offensive tackle Josh Simmons: Added noticeable weight between mandatory minicamp and now and has been impressive in one-on-ones and in the screen game.
• Receiver Andrew Armstrong: Reid said the 2025 undrafted free agent has “good speed for a big kid and good transition” quickness, which has helped him land quite a few first-team reps with other wideouts sidelined.
• Running back Brashard Smith: Getting lots of work with the first-team offense in goal-line and red-zone settings; I wasn’t sure he was a lock for the roster this summer , but the 2025 seventh-round pick seems firmly in this year’s plans.

full_text:
Blake Corum has been hard at work, starting well before dawn, to become a championship-caliber back. Jim Dedmon / Imagn Images
The Athletic has live coverage of NFL training camp .
LOS ANGELES — In the weeks before Los Angeles Rams training camp was set to begin, Blake Corum was on the opposite side of the country, challenging his body in ways he never had before.
The third-year running back was inside the Team Ascension Sports Academy in Fredericksburg, Va., where he used to drive an hour before middle school and high school at 4 a.m. Six years later, he found himself trying new movements for the first time.
In one of them, he explodes through one leg against a resistance band attached to a squat rack. In another, he props up one foot on a bench behind him with two dumbbells in each hand, then launches the planted leg.
He will also leap up from two knees to land his right foot on a foam pad, then back to an overturned BOSU ball on his left while catching a rubber weight in one hand.
These have appeared in videos that have gone viral , shared on Instagram more than 80,000 times and reaching NFL Network. And they have Rams players and coaches dreaming of what they and Corum might be able to build.
“I did see a couple of those videos,” coach Sean McVay said, “and they look cool as s—. It’s impressive. I want to see him make people miss like that in the hole.”
Corum’s inspiration to take his training to this level was about blending the old with something new. His throw-back journey began with a number change, back to his childhood 24. It continued with buying a house near his hometown of Marshall, Va., to start raising his baby daughter Zara, who was born in May.
“I just needed to go back to my roots,” Corum said.
Corum tried to wrap everything around both his roots and the newfound purpose he finds in Zara’s crib. He started doing yard work in the humidity of a Virginia summer. He cut sweets out of his diet and rewired his body clock to 3:30 a.m. alarms, all to endure the mentally and physically taxing workouts.
Teammates are starting to see glimpses of the transformation.
“He’s a lot leaner,” running back Kyren Williams said. “He looks a lot more explosive.”
One day this summer, he called Kevin Johnson, his trainer from middle school and high school, and told him he needed these workouts. They’ve helped him reflect on how he became Maryland Gatorade Player of the Year in 2019 and a four-star recruit who won a national championship at Michigan and was selected by the Rams in the third round of the 2024 NFL Draft.
The goal now is staying in an NFL that, especially for running backs, is sometimes referred to as Not For Long. Last year’s breakout of 746 rushing yards and six touchdowns on 5.1 yards per carry for the league’s No. 1 scoring offense needed to be the start of something greater.
The Rams are dreaming of a Super Bowl after the return of reigning MVP Matthew Stafford, the blockbuster additions of cornerback Trent McDuffie and two-time Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett. Corum feels the need to help. He wants to lead, not to follow.
“Reaching the NFL was a dream, but my dream is to be successful in whatever I do,” Corum said. “I’m not going to stop until I feel like I reached that success. When that day ends, I’ll stop playing football and I’ll go chase something else. But I’m not close to the success that I want in the NFL.”
Last season, Corum showcased straight-line speed and sharp vision, and grew in pass protection. But he didn’t see his body movements or the decisions behind them as elite. So Johnson designed a circuit of fast-twitch, one-leg movements designed around verbal commands.
“At the end of the day, it’s not just a power game,” Johnson said. “The NFL has plenty of power, of course. That’s the calling card. But it’s about the guys who have the balance, the control, the actual ability to plant their foot, get lateral and get linear without losing tenths of a second.”
Corum and Williams decided they needed to add explosion to Corum’s game. Corum can’t necessarily count on a Rams offensive line that was dominant, cohesive and mostly healthy last season to be the same. And he wasn’t going to be a bystander next to a passing game that can dominate with play-action, no-look passes, Puka Nacua highlights, Davante Adams touchdowns and MVP-level play from Stafford, especially if there’s any natural regression.
Williams and Corum combined for just shy of 2,000 yards last season — 1,998 to be exact — but hit a wall in the playoffs, when none of their 70 combined carries topped 20 yards. To beat elite defenses and maximize the Rams’ shift to more three-tight-end sets that pull more linebackers onto the field, both decided they needed to add a quick twitch.
So Corum stripped his process down to the basics last month. He performed most workouts barefoot, as Johnson saw the structure of shoes as a balance crutch, and on one foot, helping hone the ability to combine balance with direction and burst.
Most of all, the two trained Corum’s mind.
The NFL’s best backs can envision how to set up blocks for themselves. That skill has helped players such as Nick Chubb, Saquon Barkley, Jonathan Taylor and Bijan Robinson become the engines of their offenses in a league with many replaceable backs.
“We cannot be flat-footed,” Johnson said. “We can’t afford to. In a tenth of a second, these linebackers and D-ends and even the D-linemen are moving fast at the NFL level. We have to stay ahead of them.”
In one exercise, Corum had a leg propped up backward on a pad, or in the “piston” position, as they call it. His other was bouncing in front of him as Johnson shouted out one of three directions — left, right or middle — and in an instant, Corum shifted the bouncing foot to that spot, then back to the middle, and on and on.
One misread or misstep and the exercise would fail. It’s the sort of thing that hindered Corum’s transition to the league, from a 1,400-yard rusher at Michigan to an NFL rookie who averaged just 3.6 yards per carry. Tenths of a second can define the difference between a schemed-up 5-yard run and one that breaks for 30-plus yards — or the difference between Corum’s runs in the playoffs last year and the ones he’s looking for now.
The barefoot movements helped to centralize stress on the ankle, which has become the defining factor in Corum’s transition to what he and the team hope could be a Super Bowl-worthy back.
“We’re creating what’s called a stiff ankle. That’s when I cut and plant, I can cut on a dime, and that stiffness allows me to explode,” Corum said. “The nervous system part is about thinking while my foot is moving. That’s the type of game it is: I have to cut here, cut here, on a dime. I’m allowing my brain and my foot to work together, working that nervous system, working that fast twitch.”
Plenty of athletes come into camp in the best shape of their lives, and barefoot movements off a bench in a weight room still have to withstand the pounding and resistance of elite NFL defenses. Theory must still become reality. But if Corum’s breakout was really just the beginning of an even bigger one, perhaps those dark mornings in a gym can become something more. It all starts with a vision and a little belief.
“Everyone’s going to see the culmination of the daggone talent and the work coming together,” Johnson said. “Man, it’s going to be a blessing.”

full_text:
This spring, after years of internal and external dissection, head coach Kevin O'Connell attempted to overhaul the Vikings' run game. Michael Reaves / Getty Images
EAGAN, Minn. — You can only conceal important developments for so long in the NFL. But this aspect of the Minnesota Vikings has been kept surprisingly quiet.
If you look hard enough, past the hoopla of the quarterback competition, beyond the defense’s dominance, you can uncover a foundational difference.
This spring, after years of internal and external dissection, head coach Kevin O’Connell attempted to overhaul the Vikings’ run game.
It’s the equivalent of a Major League Baseball team think-tanking a new way to develop hitters. Staff changes preceded alterations in teaching philosophies. Coaches conveyed new training methods to players. In the last week, the Vikings have installed new elements of the playbook featuring refined personnel groupings, bespoke motion and a detailed focus on a couple of staple run concepts.
The results won’t be revealed for months. Talk can be cheap this time of year. But, already, the reaction from staffers and players has been profound.
“It’s night and day different,” left tackle Christian Darrisaw said. “You can feel it.”
This run game transformation began in earnest the day after last season ended.
Inside the locker room at the TCO Performance Center, some Vikings players filled trash bags with gear. Others hugged before departing for the offseason.
Right tackle and captain Brian O’Neill held court with reporters, answering for a sixth straight season of no playoff success. His response to a question about the rushing attack landed like an anvil.
“I thought when we were able to run the ball well, we seemed to win more games, right?” O’Neill said. “That’s kind of how it’s always been in the NFL. You have to be able to do both to have success. I thought we finished strong this year. I was proud of that. But it’s going to be on me and everybody else to try to find a dominant run game throughout the whole year .”
Yes, Minnesota ran with more effectiveness in 2025 than in previous years, by all meaningful metrics. At the same time, there was still room for growth — if the Vikings committed to the run more comprehensively.
For years, O’Connell has talked about improving the ground game. The Vikings matched his words with resources at every turn. They positioned Alexander Mattison as the starting running back in 2023, believing his ruggedness would lead to more efficiency. They signed tight end Josh Oliver with eyes on varied personnel usage. Aaron Jones’ arrival in 2024 came with higher hopes. Then, in the spring of 2025, general manager Kwesi Adofo-Mensah beefed up O’Connell’s offensive line with highly paid right guard Will Fries, veteran center Ryan Kelly and first-round left guard Donovan Jackson.
This offseason required an even more extensive excavation. The Vikings did not renew the contract of former offensive line coach Chris Kuper. As O’Connell interviewed candidates for the role, discussions with former Miami Dolphins offensive coordinator Frank Smith fleshed out the need for a new approach.
Eventually, O’Connell hired Smith, whom several players described as the brains behind most of the changes, as his assistant head coach. O’Connell also elevated assistant offensive line coach Keith Carter to replace Kuper. Carter then added Derek Warehime, a longtime collegiate O-line coach.
In February, O’Connell foreshadowed the seismic shift.
“I want to be a vertical wide-zone team,” he said at the NFL Scouting Combine in Indianapolis. “The teams that do it right are still attacking. They’re still crossing the line of scrimmage. They’re still playing on the other side of the line. (Smith and Carter) know how to do it. They know what it looks like.”
“It’s just a lot of bodies moving really fast,” linebacker Blake Cashman said.
Optimally, it’s like a massive tidal wave washing over the defensive line. Or a bullet train — five men wide — approaching at maximum velocity. During team drills in training camp, when the Vikings snap the football, the offensive linemen spring from their stances and sprint as if they’re being chased by German shepherds. While fans rattle the metal bleachers to improve their sightlines on the quarterback, the linemen blast into pads with huffs and grunts straight out of an NFL Films montage.
Carter yells constantly, and the intensity does not subside. In one drill, all of the offensive linemen gather in a large circle, and they take turns colliding with each other. In another, they link together with bungee cords, pulling in opposite directions. They are given reminders: run off the ball, inch into your second step with speed, position the backside hand with quickness, ensure correct head placement.
“The offense that we have this year is a little bit different than the offense that we had last year,” Jackson said. “In order for this to work, we have to be in great physical and mental shape.”
Darrisaw put it more plainly: “Our main focus this year is … being more aggressive. Seeing it, it f—ing makes sense.”
Other position groups are preparing with a similar purpose. Running backs repeat precise tracks, angled at the outside leg of the last blocker on the line of scrimmage. Because the running backs sprint from their stances, the quarterbacks must place the football in their arms as quickly as possible. None of this touches on half-paced reps that toy with atypical motions. It doesn’t include clever handoff techniques being practiced by the quarterbacks.
Smith brought these intricacies from Miami, where he worked with former San Francisco 49ers run-design whiz Mike McDaniel. Carter’s exposure to Kyle Shanahan’s ideology in Atlanta (and Matt LaFleur’s in Tennessee) helps the coaches disseminate the new messaging to the group.
Coaches who worked with Smith or were otherwise exposed to these types of concepts swear by their impact. The caveat is the time it takes to sync. All links in the chain (handoff, running back track and offensive line movement) need to work for the runs to explode. One mishap can ruin the momentum.
“The beauty of it is it makes everybody accountable,” Jon Embree, the former 49ers tight ends coach and one of Smith’s colleagues in Miami, said. “In this scheme, if one guy is off, it could be a bad play. That could be the difference between a touchdown and field goal. There’s pressure on everybody.”
As long as superstar receiver Justin Jefferson remains in Minnesota, the Vikings’ passing game will matter most.
This run game revolution, though, parallels the Minnesota Timberwolves’ acquisition of point guard LaMelo Ball. Like Anthony Edwards, Jefferson’s exceptionalism comes with a distinct gravity. Opposing teams will continue to focus on limiting him — unless something forces them to focus elsewhere.
Defenses shade players toward Jefferson to prevent him from ruining a game. Oftentimes, safeties will float backward into position with eyes on him. More defenders allocated to coverage means more space available in the box, and that tends to make it easier for offenses to run the ball.
The table below shows how NFL run games in 2025 were more successful versus two-high safety defenses than one-high safety defenses:
Teams such as the Los Angeles Rams, Buffalo Bills, Chicago Bears and Denver Broncos — and their thriving run games — punished defenses determined to play with two safeties in 2025. The Vikings didn’t. They faced defensive lines that were slanting and stunting, complicating on-the-fly decisions.
Injuries torpedoed the group in 2025. But Minnesota’s offense failed to make defenses pay for leaning into this strategy when Sam Darnold was the quarterback, too.
“There were times in the past where we weren’t running off the ball,” Darrisaw said. “We were thinking more. Now, it’s just full speed. Let’s go move the line of scrimmage and see what happens.”
This new iteration of the offense will hinge on pre-snap eye candy…

title: Eagles O-linemen embrace 'O-line-friendly' scheme. What's different and how will they improve? Arguably the Eagles' greatest strength, the offensive line has high regard for Sean Mannion's new scheme. Zach Berman 14

full_text:
Philadelphia Eagles offensive tackle Lane Johnson, left, and guard Landon Dickerson at training camp at Jefferson Health Training Complex. Johnson has missed the past four practices for personal reasons unrelated to an injury. Terence Lewis / Icon Sportswire via Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — In January 2025, Lane Johnson responded to a perceived snub on the All-Pro rosters by displaying a sheet of paper on his locker stall with a side-by-side comparison of Johnson and the tackle who earned more votes. Among the list of nine data points was “Island Rate” — the percentage of snaps in which Johnson was one-on-one on an island against the pass rusher. Johnson had the highest percentage in the NFL. He became accustomed to being trusted to block one-on-one throughout the past 13 seasons. The challenge became a point of pride.
“I’ve never had help in my entire career in pass protection here,” Johnson said.
The Eagles changed their offensive scheme this offseason when they hired new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion. The staff shuffle included the departure of long-time offensive line coach Jeff Stoutland, one of the NFL’s most celebrated assistant coaches and the only position coach for whom all five Eagles starters ever played. He was replaced by Chris Kuper . The overhaul has had a pronounced effect across the offense. But the biggest adjustment might be on the offensive line — perhaps the best group on the Eagles’ roster and a foundation of their success during the past decade.
It’s still the honeymoon period, but early reviews from truth-telling offensive linemen offer consensus approval — including Johnson noting the joys of guard help in pass protection.
“It’s very O-line-friendly compared to maybe some past years I’ve been involved in,” Johnson said.
“I agree,” Mailata said. “Stretching the defense a lot more than we did in the past. It’s not a knock to our past schemes and our past coaches. … Stress them out a lot more — they don’t know if it’s a pass or a run. And the play-action game being married is pretty key to the scheme.”
The sentiment of the “O-line-friendly” scheme has been shared by all five starting linemen. Of course, the previous schemes seemed to accentuate the offensive linemen. The Eagles reached the Super Bowl twice in the past four seasons. They paved the way for a 2,000-yard rusher in 2024 and a 1,000-yard rusher in each of the past four years. Four of the five starting linemen are among the top-10 highest-paid players at their positions. Three earned Pro Bowl honors. Two earned All-Pro honors. It’s not as if the offensive line responsibilities were a major problem before, although there was regression last year while injuries plagued the line and the offense grew stale.
The linemen always carried considerable responsibility before the snap — not even to mention what happened after the snap. When you watched an Eagles game, you would often see hand motions and nonstop communication at the line of scrimmage. They were a synchronized machine, with experience playing together and a seemingly advanced degree in making adjustments. Jason Kelce excelled in this area.
In the new scheme, there’s less required at the line of scrimmage from the group. Communication is still important, but one message has been that they want to force the defense to react to them.
“From the standpoint of not going up there and playing chess, we can play a little faster,” center Cam Jurgens said. “This scheme presses a defense, and you’re able to play fast and not overthink things. You can play a little quicker. And you’re making things look a little more complex without having to think more complex. It’s kind of a nice intermediate, best of both worlds where we can play fast but not have to think a million miles an hour. So I really like it so far.”
When asked about pre-snap calls, Jurgens said he’ll still make calls and go through his reads, but “it’s a little bit less diagnosing and playing a chess game with the defense.”
“We want to catch them off guard with everything we do, and we don’t want to be predictable, and we want to be able to play fast without them knowing what we’re doing,” Jurgens said.
Left guard Landon Dickerson explained a key will be “eliminating the slow play” of getting to the line of scrimmage and making adjustments while the play clock nears expiration. The Eagles ranked No. 30 in the NFL last season in time on the clock when the ball was snapped. Dickerson said the Eagles want to be able to make a call, stick with the call and run the play. He noted how Vic Fangio’s defense likes to move around and flummox the offense, a strategy that’s spread around the league.
“If you can get up there quick and run your plays and not rely on what they’re doing, it makes your life a little easier,” Dickerson said.
Once the ball is snapped, the responsibilities change as well. Johnson pointed to staples of the offense that differed from what the Eagles majored in during past seasons: the quarterback taking the snap from under center, a higher rate of under-center play action and a wide zone running game. From an offensive lineman’s perspective, Johnson said the benefit of playing with the quarterback under center is that the defense has a more difficult time determining if it’s a run or a play action.
That allows the linemen to get off the ball sooner because there’s hesitation and reading of the defense. The offensive linemen must be consistent with their presentation to the defense, including their stance.
Johnson said that has included more three-point stances than in recent seasons because they need to keep a “low hat” to sell the play. And then when the running back (or quarterback) is moving, so are the linemen.
“A lot of our landmarks are really wide,” Johnson said. “Outside zone and a lot of the run game are built on backside cutoff blocks by the guard and center and tackle. If the running game can stretch the front side and get around the edge, do it. If you can’t, run the ‘S’ pattern and ride the wave backside. It’s a lot of fun. Just for us, me and Jordan are getting to run, stretch the field, cover some yardage; so that way it tires out defenses, makes them cover each gap. All the fakes, motions look the same, hard to differentiate, makes guys hesitate.”
The Eagles’ offensive linemen are bigger than most linemen in this type of scheme, although they have the athletic ability to move in space. Johnson and Mailata are extraordinary athletes for tackles. Johnson set combine records in 2013 . Mailata was a rugby player in Australia. Still, Mailata noted the increased emphasis on conditioning during training camp to prepare them to move in space. That’s long been a specialty of Jurgens, who was Kelce’s successor at center and possesses the same movement skills. (Dickerson, who is 6 feet 6 and 332 pounds, said he did not lose any notable weight this offseason. “Not more than a big trip to the bathroom,” he said.)
Another change is adjusting to differences in the cadence. There’s been a higher rate of pre-snap penalties early in training camp as the team adjusts, though that is presumably an early-August concern that will be resolved once the group spends time together.
Spending time together is key. For all the changes in the scheme, the best improvement might come from healthier players. Jurgens and Dickerson were coming off surgeries last summer after an arduous run to the Super Bowl. Dickerson even underwent surgery during training camp and rushed back. Johnson suffered an injury during the season that limited him to 10 games. The group entered camp notably healthier than last offseason. (Dickerson and Jurgens even traveled to Colombia for stem cell therapy.) Better health might be the key development. If they had been healthier in 2024, there might not have been as much of a push for an offensive overhaul.
“We have all our guys out there for Day 1, that’s big,” Johnson said on the first day of camp. “A lot of people depending on us, so we…

full_text:
Brock Purdy is healthy, but several teammates are sitting out with minor injuries, leaving the 49ers short on numbers. Sergio Estrada / Imagn Images
The Athletic has live coverage of NFL training camp .
SANTA CLARA, Calif. — Health is in the eye of the beholder, apparently.
The San Francisco 49ers had 20 players not participating by the end of Wednesday’s practice (not including receiver Ricky Pearsall, who is on injured reserve and out for the season ). That’s 22.2 percent of the roster hanging out in the trainer’s room nursing injuries.
Would that mean Tuesday’s joint practice in Santa Clara against the Tennessee Titans — two days before the preseason opener at Levi’s Stadium — is in jeopardy?
Phooey, said assistant head coach Chris Foerster, who continues to lead the team in place of the injured Kyle Shanahan .
“It seems like we’re very healthy,” Foerster said. “We have injuries. We have dings, bumps and bruises, and guys are missing practices. It has yet to come up in anything I’ve heard. It doesn’t mean it hasn’t been discussed, but you have two players deep at every position, and you can practice.”
For the skeptics out there, the 49ers did cancel their joint practice with the New Orleans Saints in 2024 when they were down 23 players.
Though receivers Mike Evans (quad) and De’Zhaun Stribling (hamstring) remained out with apparent minor nicks, there was a new list of players sidelined Wednesday. Fullback Kyle Juszczyk broke his finger, receiver Jacob Cowing strained his hip flexor, and rookie offensive lineman Carver Willis suffered a concussion. Defensive end Sam Okuayinonu and guard Nick Zakelj seemed to get hurt during practice.
Meanwhile, defensive end Nick Bosa, defensive tackle Osa Odighizuwa and linebacker Dre Greenlaw sat out the session with what the team described as “soreness.” All three are considered day to day.
Foerster said injuries can be a good thing, as they allow reserve players to get more snaps in practice, but what else is he supposed to say?
• Brock Purdy was sharp Wednesday, even though most of his top pass catchers are nursing injuries. He was 13 of 15 in 11-on-11 situations, including a deep-ball touchdown up the left sideline to Jordan Watkins toward the end of practice.
Purdy was also effective in a red zone drill midway through the session, scoring on three straight plays: a short pass to tailback Patrick Taylor Jr., who slipped out of the backfield and went uncovered; a quarterback run to the right pylon; and a short pass to a sliding Junior Bergen, who’s made a lot of gritty catches in recent practices.
Mac Jones, meanwhile, connected with Watkins in the end zone on a crossing route in the same drill and went 10 of 16 in 11-on-11 scenarios.
• With Evans, Stribling and Cowing not practicing, Watkins was a popular target for the quarterbacks. The second-year receiver saw five passes his way. He let a deep attempt from Adrian Martinez go through his hands, and another pass might have been a completion had he extended his arms and not allowed cornerback Deommodore Lenoir to break up the pass. The other three targets ended with catches, and it’s clear the quarterbacks trust him to get open in practice.
• Veteran cornerback Jack Jones continues to make plays, including breaking up one pass from Purdy to Malik Turner and another from Martinez that Jones knocked into the air. The fluttering ball was gathered in by rookie linebacker Jaden Dugger and run back for a would-be defensive touchdown.
• There was a small shakeup among the offensive starters Wednesday, with Robert Jones taking all of the first-team snaps at left guard and Conner Colby, the top left guard to this point in camp, working with the second stringers.
Foerster said the initial plan was to give Colby snaps at right guard and Jones and Willis snaps at left guard so they could match up against different opponents. That approach, however, fell apart when Willis suffered a concussion and Brett Toth had to sit out practice with an undisclosed injury.
“I was going to do a lot more interior-wise, so it wouldn’t just look like it was flipping the two guys, but it didn’t work out with the injuries,” Foerster said.
• Among the 49ers who have been part of every practice so far: left tackle Trent Williams, who turned 38 in July, and running back Christian McCaffrey, who turned 30 in June. Foerster noted both are being limited to 20 snaps per practice.
“You always have to be careful that reps in July don’t take away from reps in January,” Foerster said.
Austen Pleasants has filled in at left tackle when Williams sits out a series. With Jordan James (ribs), Kaelon Black (adductor) and Isaac Guerendo (pectoral) sidelined, Taylor, Sincere McCormick and Khalil Herbert have served as McCaffrey’s backups.
• Some good news in the injury department? Defensive tackle Alfred Collins was worked into team drills for the first time after offseason shoulder surgery. Rookie defensive tackle Gracen Halton was also back at practice Wednesday. He looked quick in blowing past Zakelj in one-on-one pass-rush drills. After the win, Halton got dapped up by his defensive line teammates … and by Williams, who strolled over to compliment the rookie.
• Among the injured players, Stribling (hamstring) and safety Malik Mustapha (hamstring) appear closest to a return. Both were sprinting at full speed Wednesday.
• With Greenlaw out, Garret Wallow took snaps at weakside linebacker next to Fred Warner. Nick Martin stuck to his usual strongside spot.
• The team portion of practice began with a big defensive play — defensive tackle CJ West burst through the offensive line and crashed into McCaffrey for a would-be tackle for loss. Two plays later, Warner snuffed out a McCaffrey run to the outside for no gain.
• The 49ers signed receiver KhaDarel Hodge and defensive end Ogbo Okoronkwo to one-year deals and waived defensive tackle Kevin Givens and defensive end Cam Sample. Okoronkwo played under defensive coordinator Raheem Morris with the Los Angeles Rams in 2021.

full_text:
Tampa Bay Buccaneers defensive tackle Vita Vea recently requested a trade after contract extension talks with the team stalled. Mark Konezny / Imagn Images
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers do not plan to trade Vita Vea, despite the defensive tackle’s recent request, general manager Jason Licht told reporters Thursday.
News broke last week that Vea asked for a trade after contract extension talks with Tampa Bay had stalled. Vea, a two-time Pro Bowler, is in the final season of a four-year, $71 million contract extension he signed in 2022.
“I have no plans of trading Vita,” Licht said at Thursday’s training camp. “We love Vita. We’ve been engaged with his agent. I don’t know how it’s going to end, but we’ve been engaged with his agent.”
Vea attended, but did not participate in, the Bucs’ mandatory minicamp last month. The 31-year-old has not participated in training camp, but Licht said it’s precautionary because Vea has a minor back injury.
Vea has spent his entire NFL career with the Buccaneers, who drafted him in the first round in 2018. He’s appeared in 112 regular-season games (107 starts) and eight playoff games. After winning four consecutive NFC South titles, the Buccaneers fell just short of another last season after finishing 8-9, losing the tiebreaker to the Carolina Panthers.
This offseason, Licht made several aggressive defensive upgrades by drafting edge Rueben Bain Jr. and linebacker Josiah Trotter. He also signed several veterans, including linebacker Alex Anzalone, defensive tackle A’Shawn Robinson and defensive lineman Rakeem Nunez-Roches. Vea is set to be at the heart of that revamped unit.
But Vea isn’t the only Bucs player unhappy with his contract situation, as quarterback Baker Mayfield said last week that he felt “disrespected” and “undervalued” during extension talks with the team this offseason.
Mayfield, 31, said he set the deadline for an extension to get done before training camp began. He added that the team made him offers, but he wanted to be compensated like a franchise quarterback.
When asked Thursday if the team views Mayfield as such, Licht said, “We think he is. We love Baker. Our feelings for Baker haven’t changed.”
Mayfield will play out the final year of the three-year, $100 million deal he signed in 2024. The Buccaneers could use the franchise tag on Mayfield in 2027, but Licht said they would rather not and continue working toward a long-term extension.
Mayfield has a 27-24 record as the Bucs’ QB and led them to the playoffs as NFC South champions in 2023 and 2024, two seasons in which he also earned Pro Bowl nods. He had a down year in 2025 while playing through injuries, and Tampa Bay lost five of its final six games.

full_text:
Jayden Daniels has given the Washington Commanders reason to smile at the start of training camp. Scott Taetsch / Getty Images
ASHBURN, Va. — The narrative changed, and it changed fast.
The first couple of training camp practices for the Washington Commanders at times looked eerily similar to last year’s camp. The sessions were relatively short and limited to mostly red zone work without full pads, so it was impossible to get a complete picture of the offense. But what Washington did show wasn’t pretty.
Many of Jayden Daniels’ pass attempts were either slightly late or dropped by his receivers, and the defense capitalized. Training camp is often deceiving — remember when rookie cornerback Emmanuel Forbes appeared otherworldly at the start of camp in 2023? — but the early going this year amplified Washington’s roster shortcomings on offense.
By Monday, when the Commanders strapped on pads for the first time, the tide shifted.
Coach Dan Quinn was asked before that practice whether any player had stood out in the first stretch of camp, and he said Daniels had appeared even further ahead than he expected in taking control of a new offense.
Then Daniels validated his words with his finest showing of camp, which he followed with two more impressive days to help close the gap between the offense and defense.
“With him, it’s really easy,” tight end Chig Okonkwo said. “You just gotta be where you’re supposed to be and he’ll find you with an accurate ball.”
Quinn divided this year’s training camp into six blocks, each stressing different components. The first four days began a lengthy ramp-up that focused mostly on red zone. The latest stretch emphasized play from 30 yards in, with some situational work, such as end-of-game and two-minute scenarios, which allowed Daniels to showcase his decision-making and accuracy, two hallmarks of his Offensive Rookie of the Year season in 2024.
“He has the ability to pinpoint the ball into the right location,” Quinn said Wednesday. “He’s always had that trait. Now, in a new system, (the question was) can he even elevate that further? So, that’s the command that I’m looking for from those spots, and that’s the thing I would say right now that’s so impressive to me.”
Since he arrived in Washington, Daniels has made a point of spending extra time on the field after practices to get more reps with his receivers and work on the finer details of routes and timing. That has continued, and seems to have paid early dividends.
One of Daniels’ most impressive throws of camp was on a deep ball to Terry McLaurin that sailed over the head of cornerback Mike Sainristil and fell perfectly into the receiver’s arms in stride.
“That’s not luck,” Quinn said. “That’s super hard to do. But the amount of unseen work to have that throw is evident.”
Daniels has had many others that have been just as impressive, including a deep ball over the middle to Luke McCaffrey , another in the back of the end zone to McLaurin and one over the heads of two defenders to tight end Colson Yankoff that probably should’ve been ruled complete.
Daniels has so far appeared to be an even better version of the player he was a couple years ago, when he helped mask some of Washington’s deficiencies to guide it to the NFC Championship Game.
But unlike 2024, Daniels may finally have a more complete roster, thanks to general manager Adam Peters’ latest move.
Here’s what else we’ve gleaned from the start of camp:
Washington has another veteran receiver. Finally.
The Commanders on Wednesday agreed to terms on a one-year deal with Stefon Diggs worth up to $12 million, according to a league source who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
The move gives Washington another proven wideout who can complement McLaurin in the pass game, provides Daniels another reliable target after the team moved on from Deebo Samuel and tight end Zach Ertz, and offers Diggs a chance to play at home. Win. Win. Win.
Washington has tried for years to fill that so-called “No. 2” receiving role (Quinn doesn’t care for that label but I’m struggling to come up with a better one), leaving McLaurin to carry the brunt of the workload and forcing Daniels to often play Superman, which was especially apparent last year as injuries tested the Commanders’ depth.
They entered camp this year with perhaps more depth at receiver, after re-signing Dyami Brown and Treylon Burks and adding Van Jefferson and rookie Antonio Williams. But that group had no clear leader and no one outside of McLaurin with consistent starting experience.
The team, according to league sources who were granted anonymity for their candor on the matter, once viewed Brandon Aiyuk as a potential fit if the 49ers released him, but he remains under contract and after months of criticizing his general manager, head coach, former agent and even Daniels on social media, his odds of landing in Washington diminished.
The focus then shifted to Diggs, who had been in communication with the team for a while before agreeing to terms.
His first practice as a Commander will be Friday.
The arrival of Diggs shores up the receiver group, but two key positions are still shaky: center and cornerback.
Nick Allegretti has been out for most of camp because of a calf strain, creating concern about the team’s depth on the interior. Julian Good-Jones has been Allegretti’s primary fill-in with the ones, but he’s played only two offensive snaps in his NFL career, and his inexperience has shown. Washington also has rookie Matt Gulbin and signed former Bengals lineman Trey Hill for depth.
Quinn said he didn’t expect Allegretti’s injury to sideline him long term, but his absence has raised the question of how the team will fare if he gets injured in season. The answer so far hasn’t been promising.
Cornerback, however, may be even more concerning. Trey Amos still hasn’t returned to the field after suffering a fractured fibula in early November, which leaves him little time to get back into football shape for the season once he’s medically cleared. Washington brought in veteran Rasul Douglas for additional help, and recently signed Fabian Moreau following Ahkello Witherspoon’s abrupt retirement.
But given the Commanders’ defensive shortcomings in recent years, it’s fair to wonder if that’s enough.
“One of the things that Trey’s excellent at, he can play on and off the ball,” Quinn said. “And so, in this system, when do you wanna be down? When do you wanna be off? It’s all a big part of the disguise. So, when Trey’s working off to the side, honestly, like right now, a lot of the drill work is specific to what do the guys do today so he can almost mirror that to the side. So, he’s got a lot of versatility. Obviously, he’s got size and you feel that at the line of scrimmage a lot. But we’re excited to get back rolling with him.”
When the Commanders selected Sonny Styles at No. 7 in the draft, it seemed likely that he would be the primary “mike” linebacker, tasked with the green dot. Sure, he’s a rookie and calling plays on top of learning everything else can make for a tough transition to the NFL. But if any rookie seemed built for it, it was him.
But Quinn never publicly tabbed one player to wear the green dot; he repeatedly said it would depend on the defensive package on the field and who seemed most comfortable in the role. He also said it could be a linebacker or a defensive back.
After a week of camp, the primary guy has been Frankie Luvu.
Luvu boasts the most experience in that role, having worn the green dot in Carolina before signing with Washington in 2024.
“I love it,” Luvu said. “I did it when I was in Carolina, and it’s just in that matter of, ‘Hey, get the calls and get the guys ready. Now what you got?’ That’s kind of my mentality, looking at what down it is, what package we’re in, then looking at what I’ve got to do and get the call.”

title: Here's Exactly What the Cardinals Want to See From Carson Beck Tonight
full_text:
ARIZONA — It's the Carson Beck show tonight.
The Arizona Cardinals named the rookie quarterback their starter for the NFL's Hall of Fame Game against the Carolina Panthers. Beck is expected to play roughly a half before Kedon Slovis assumes duties the rest of the night.
There's so much intrigue around Beck and what the third-round pick can become in the desert, though tonight will be the first of many stepping stones in helping the Cardinals figure out exactly what they have in their new quarterback.
Beck, set to make his unofficial NFL debut tonight at 5:00 PM AZ time on NBC, simply needs to keep the offense moving on schedule according to multiple coaches.
Head coach Mike LaFleur is confident Beck can efficiently operate the Cardinals' offense.
"Clean operation and make the right play for the Cardinals in that time," he said when asked what he's looking for out of Beck.
"We're not overly game-planning. You go into this game with you could say plays that that no matter what they bring are going to be protected, both in the run game and the pass game. It might be hot and stuff like that, but you're always going to have answers. You're not going to have game-plan, gimmicky plays. So it's plays that you know all these guys have ran multiple times, whether it be OTAs, training camp, walkthroughs, all that.
"... But hey, go out there, operate that huddle. There's no coaching behind you right there, which I have no question that he's going to do that. He's done a great job with the operation. He's super smart. He hears it well. He says it well. He visualizes it well. And then when that ball's snapped, just make the right play for the Cardinals. Make the right, sound quarterback decision. Might be ditching the ball. Might be throwing one. Might be ripping through a progression. It might be protecting it if we get a quick beat, whatever it might be. So take it one play at a time, and we'll grade it as such."
Beck's profile as an NFL-ready passer made him a viable option for the Cardinals in the third round. His stature (6-4), game management ability and familiarity with NFL-style operations thanks to his experiences at Georgia and Miami have made him an intriguing prospect for Arizona to evaluate.
LaFleur also added tonight won't swing the pendulum in either direction based off Beck's performance - good or bad.
"You're never going to put too much stock into it," he added.
"You just [say] 'hey, this is the play that we gave you. This is the defense they gave you.' Did our 10 guys do all the right stuff? Carson could be doing everything right, but two guys messed up, and then it's going to look like Carson made the mistake, right? And so that's just the price of playing quarterback. So again, you just take it one play at a time and grade it as such."
The good news for Beck? There's no pressure to win a starting job right away, at least not with Jacoby Brissett and Gardner Minshew in store. He previously told us he wasn't nervous after finding out about the start, which you can read more about here .
However, tonight's game is still significant in the eyes of offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett.
"Everything's about the game. I mean, it's that simple," said Hackett.
"... So I think this is going to be great for all of us to see them, to see how we respond with them, coach them in those situations because you can practice, but there's never the pressure that comes from being on a big scale game like this. I know it's a preseason, it's the first game, but golly, it's a great stage, it's a great experience. This is going to be my fourth one, so we're going to learn a lot about all the guys that are out there."

title: A New Era of Cardinals Football (Unofficially) Starts Now
full_text:
ARIZONA — An unproven coach gets his start in football's most coveted destination.
The two ends of the football spectrum couldn't be more opposite for Arizona Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur and the beginning of his coaching career. LaFleur, a first-timer in the seat, will oversee the Cardinals in the NFL's Hall of Fame Game tonight — an obvious pinnacle for anybody who's privileged enough to be involved in the game.
It's not an official start. A win or loss won't go into the official column for LaFleur's coaching career, but this is the first time LaFleur will be on the sidelines leading the Cardinals.
And you can't tell him these games don't matter.
"Just because it's preseason and the win/loss doesn't count, it doesn't mean that this isn't real football," LaFleur told reporters this week.
LaFleur represents a massive breath of fresh air after Jonathan Gannon. Besides the fact of both being first-time coaches, LaFleur arrives with the profile of an innovative offensive play-caller that's studied under two of the league's best minds in Sean McVay and Kyle Shanahan. He's got the NFC West experience coveted to compete in football's toughest division and in terms of potential, there weren't many out there matching his ceiling.
The Cardinals, after whiffing on Gannon, needed a massive swing at the plate. LaFleur was just that, and if he pays off, Arizona could very well turn the unfortunate tide of the franchise. The Cardinals haven't made the playoffs since 2021 and haven't won the division since 2015.
None of that changes tonight, not even close, though this is a proverbial warm-up swing for LaFleur to get his feet wet as a head coach.
"Never assume anything," LaFleur said on being a head coach before going into what's surprised him the most about being in his spot.
"The answer I keep going to is when you get asked what color markers you want for your board and where the boards go, it's like put the board on the wall and give me the markers that work. Like what are we talking about? Keep the main thing, the main thing. It's football, but again, you do have those things that come across your desk, and you have to roll with it."
To most eyes, Thursday night will be a brief stint of watching. Some will lose interest after Carson Beck departs action. Others will turn the channel at halftime while different folks may just stick around for the whole thing.
Not many would classify tonight as must-see TV.

title: Josh Sweat 'Locked In' As Cardinals Return Draws Closer
full_text:
ARIZONA — Arizona Cardinals outside linebacker Josh Sweat was never going to suit up for the team in Thursday's Hall of Fame Game matchup, especially after head coach Mike LaFleur told reporters roughly 35 players wouldn't be playing against the Panthers.
However, the Cardinals' pass rusher hasn't logged a practice in 2026. Not at offseason team activities — or mandatory minicamp — or training camp.
Several concerns around Sweat, his management of his knee injury and potential unhappiness around the organization dating back to a reported trade request months ago have all fueled speculation from the outside.
From the inside, however, the Cardinals insist Sweat's trending in the right direction.
"He's locked in right now with everything. Meetings and post-practice tape and all that stuff," Cardinals defensive coordinator Nick Rallis told reporters this week.
"He's the same Sweaty. Like, funny guy when you're not talking ball, but locked in. Leader, all of that."
Sweat, 29, paced the Cardinals in sacks last season with no close second-place contender. His importance to Arizona's pass rush can't be overstated.
Head coach Mike LaFleur gave a three-word , "Yes. I do." answer when asked if he was still confident Sweat would be ready for the regular season.
While we haven't seen Sweat, the Cardinals say he's active in his role with the team and he looks ready to return soon.
"He's in all the meetings. He's around. I know I've said it, so broken record there, but he looks really good in terms of [being] healthy, in shape, all those kind of things," LaFleur said today.
"He's putting a lot of work in behind the scenes to make sure when he gets the green light and everyone feels good. Ultimately [we're] making sure Josh feels good both mentally and physically to go out there and perform the way [he can] because he takes a lot of pride in what his product looks like. That tape matters a lot to him as I've gotten to know him. So he's earned the right to communicate with us to say, 'hey, I feel good, I'm ready to go.'"
That likely means no preseason action for the eight-year veteran, but what really matters is Sweat is healthy for the regular season opener in Los Angeles.
LaFleur doubled down on Sweat suiting up in Week 1.
"But again, whether you believe me or not, I'm not worried about him come September 13th at all."
